title: Stand firm
hookLine: the good lies in the will, so stand firm there (Discourses 1.29)
carry: let the branches move in the wind

cards: A tree in a storm doesn't stay still. The branches thrash, leaves tear off, the whole crown bends sideways. What keeps it standing is underneath, out of sight: the roots, gripping the ground.

A tree that tried to hold every leaf in place would snap. Epictetus has a whole chapter on constancy, on staying steady when pressure comes, and his advice runs the same way as the tree's. Know where your roots are.

teach.h: THE GOOD IS A STATE OF THE WILL.
teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-nine, on constancy. It opens with a short, dense claim. The good, Epictetus says, is a certain state of the will, and so is the bad.
Everything outside the will, money, health, reputation, even the body, is material the will works with.
Earlier in the Discourses he puts it this way: as wood is the carpenter's material, each person's own life is the material of the art of living.

The carpenter isn't good because the wood is fine, but because of what he does with it. That's where the roots are. If your good lives in your will, pressure on everything else is weather in the branches.
A threat to your job, your comfort, your standing: those are leaves, real and worth caring about, but not the roots. Then Epictetus imagines the test. Someone powerful threatens you.
Don't panic, he says; ask what is being threatened. If it's the body or the property, the will is still standing.
He even pictures God calling a student forward as a witness: come and testify for me. Is anything outside the will good or bad? Will you show up and say it, or tremble and say the opposite?
Constancy isn't stiffness, or refusing to feel the wind. It's knowing which part of you is supposed to move and which isn't.
The week in a breath: never alone, blind, not wicked, a clay lamp, not my judgment, test the coin, a good opponent, and now stand firm.

how: Some Stoic practitioners prepare for pressure by naming in advance what could be lost and what couldn't, and anchoring themselves in their own choices.

o: refuse to feel anything when trouble comes
never change your mind once you've made a choice
keep steady in the will, while outside things bend

p: like a life: material for living

s: Epictetus says constancy means feeling nothing
constancy is knowing which part moves and which doesn't, not refusing to feel.
Epictetus compares a person's life to a carpenter's wood
material for the art of living; the good is in what the will does with it.
for Epictetus, the good lives in the will
so pressure on everything else is weather in the branches.

games.q: someone powerful threatens you. you're Epictetus' student. what's the first thing to ask?
o: how do I get out of this?
games.why: if it's the body or the property, the will is still standing, and that's where the good lives.

practice: Feel your feet flat on the floor, the ground solid under you. Let one pressure blow through like wind, a deadline, a hard conversation, someone's expectations, and notice what bends: plans, comfort, mood.
Then come back to your feet, and to what doesn't need to bend: what you value, how you mean to act.

wordCard.voice: Stand firm. Epictetus' constancy: the good lives in the will, so let the branches move in the wind and keep the roots where they are.

orig.note: Greek eustatheia: steadiness, standing well; the title word of Discourses 1.29.

carryVoice: Your line: let the branches move in the wind. The roots are yours. Day four hundred six, and the week is whole.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.15 (wood as the carpenter's material, life as the material of the art of living)
